scenes: The engine keeps what it knows in small tables.
This is the table of computers.
Each row is one computer: its number, its name, what you want it to be, and what the engine last saw.
You click Start in the app.
The app starts nothing itself.
It sends a call, start computer seven, into one queue.
Everything that can change the state enters through that queue, one at a time.
The core is a function.
It reads the state and the call, and checks that computer seven exists and is stopped.
Then it returns three things: the new state, an event, and an effect.
The effect is only a request.
A driver does the real work: it starts the virtual machine.
That takes time, and it can fail.
When it is done, its answer comes back through the same queue, as an input.
The core handles that input the same way.
It writes seen running, and a second event.
What you want and what the engine saw now agree, so there is nothing left to do.
The core touches nothing.
So the same inputs, in the same order, always give the same result: the engine can replay a history, and pick up after a crash.
The numbered events are how the app follows what the engine did.
What agents do inside a computer is not in them: that is the record, and it is written apart.
And the core can be tested with millions of random sequences of inputs before it ever starts a real machine.
